item.title: Psychedelics: Are We Repeating Timothy Leary’s Mistakes?
item.description:
Addiction

Psychedelics: Are We Repeating Timothy Leary’s Mistakes?

From 1960s psychedelic research to Oregon psilocybin centers and FDA submissions.

Posted November 27, 2026

Key points
  • Timothy Leary's story showed what happens when psychedelic advocacy outruns science.
  • The psychedelic trip ends. Its psychological consequences may not. Who cares for the patient?
  • Neuroplasticity is not always therapeutic. Changing a brain isn’t the same as treating illness.
  • Psychedelic-induced suggestibility may facilitate therapy, but it may also facilitate exploitation.

Today's psychedelic renaissance traces back to Timothy Leary, the colorful Harvard psychologist whose slogan, “Turn on, tune in, drop out,” became a prescription for the counterculture.

Today, in an era of ubiquitous artificial intelligence (AI) and brain studies, looking to the 1960s for answers seems almost quaint. But history has its uses, especially if we seem determined to repeat it.

Leary Lesson One: Advocacy Isn’t Science

Professors Leary and Alpert led the Harvard Psilocybin Project, highlighting potential therapeutic and mystical applications of psychedelics like psilocybin for treating addiction, anxiety, and depression.

But advocacy increasingly overshadowed research. Leary's Concord Prison Experiment suggested psilocybin reduced criminal recidivism. Later evaluations—like a 34-year follow-up of the Concord Prison Experiment—found claims of lasting treatment effects were erroneous.

By 1963, Harvard dismissed Leary. He was obsessed with personal intoxication and circumventing both student safeguards and academic caution. His counterculture advocacy helped trigger a strong cultural backlash and subsequent psychedelic criminalization.

Today’s psychedelic trials avoid Leary’s mistakes by emphasizing strict screening, clinical oversight, and controlled settings.

And modern psychiatry has great hopes for psychedelics. Yet psychedelic trials face distinctive challenges. For example, patients know when they receive the active drug, and their expectations influence outcomes. Therapists also may be true believers.

Meanwhile, the RAND Psychedelics Survey estimates that roughly 11 million American adults used psilocybin in the past year. But support is greatest for FDA approval. Approval for psilocybin among military veterans was only 24% for general legal use but 54% for FDA-approved therapy. Yet passing legislation, opening psychedelic centers, and obtaining FDA approval are very different accomplishments.

Lesson Two: Oregon Ballot Measure 109

Oregon voters approved the measure, and psilocybin centers opened in 2023. Adults 21 years and older (including out-of-state visitors) may access services with no medical diagnosis, prescription, or referral.

Unlike a retail cannabis dispensary, clients can’t buy takeout mushrooms. Instead, services require a mandatory preparation session, on-site administration of up to 50 mg of psilocybin under the supervision of a state-licensed facilitator, and an optional follow-up integration session.

An August 2026 JAMA Network Open study of 346 participants at 24 licensed centers by P. Todd Korthuis, MD, and colleagues offers a landmark real-world dataset and cautionary tale for policymakers.

Participants described improvements in depression, anxiety, PTSD symptoms, well-being, and life satisfaction. But there was no control group, randomization, or representative patient population.

Also, 4 participants (1.2%), psychedelic novices, experienced serious behavioral adverse reactions requiring emergency care.

However, 3 of the 4 participants who experienced serious adverse reactions nevertheless described their experience as highly meaningful.

Meaningful? Certainly. Therapeutic? Not necessarily.

A separate WUSTL mystery-shopper study found that centers took screening seriously. I previously reviewed this study in detail.

Although legally framed around general personal growth and wellness, Oregon data show the vast majority of clients seek services for specific mental health struggles. According to the OPS 2025 Year in Review, the top reported reasons for seeking psilocybin were anxiety, depression, PTSD, and other trauma.

Three months from treatment, 4.5% of participants reported persistent/worsening depression, 1.9% reported thoughts of death or suicide, and 8.7% reported symptoms suggesting possible hallucinogen-persisting perception disorder (HPPD).

When the Trip Is Over, Who Cares for the Patient?

A recent NPR report highlighted severe, lingering psychological destabilization in some patients following psychedelic clinical trials. Yet post-psychedelic risks, ranging from panic attacks to suicidal ideation and dissociation, are frequently overlooked.

Psychiatrist and neuroscientist David Rabin wrote in the Los Angeles Times that roughly half his clinical time is spent helping patients recover from challenging drug experiences. Some patients are frightened or disconnected. Others believe they discovered universal truths. As Rabin put it, “Certainty is a hell of a drug.”

Patients may suffer from persistent anxiety, perceptual disturbances, psychiatric deterioration, or destabilization of their understanding of themselves and reality. Prior screening before taking psychedelics cannot accurately identify everyone at risk.

In addiction medicine, we learned long ago that successful detoxification isn’t the same as recovery from addiction. Similarly, completing a psychedelic session and not experiencing an emergency isn’t itself evidence of long-term safety.

Two new neuroscience studies deserve attention.

Gudmundsen and colleagues, reporting in Nature Communications, found distinct metabolic effects of psilocybin, LSD, and 2C-B in rats, with modest, drug-dependent changes detectable one week later. Only some changes were shared across all three drugs. A healthy person who takes 2C-B and one who takes psilocybin don’t run the same risks.

In Science Advances, Delgado-Sallent and colleagues in BU's Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences reported that psilocybin and ketamine altered decision-making strategies and orbitofrontal activity in mice. At selected doses, decisions became slower but more accurate, suggesting that psychedelics change brain-wide configurations and local dynamics to promote more deliberate, flexible, and sensory-driven decisions.

Neither study establishes human brain injury, and neither shows lasting clinical benefits. But there are known and unknown risks with psychedelics. Treating severe illness justifies accepting some risk and uncertainty.

Psychedelics appear to change the brain. But who needs their brain changed?

Opening a window for change doesn't determine what’s actually learned in the experience. In a clinical setting, therapy shapes that window. At a party, a retreat, or with a charismatic guide, something else may climb through that window of opportunity; for example, psychedelics may unmask psychosis or mania in someone who looked and felt fine.

Lesson Three: Ethics in an Altered State

Insights may feel valid without being true.

Psychedelics increase emotional openness, suggestibility, and trust. These characteristics may facilitate therapy. Alternatively, sometimes they facilitate exploitation.

Undue influence and misconduct are potential problems. People in a highly suggestible state are easier to exploit.

A 2024 JAMA Network Open consensus statement led by Amy McGuire addressed informed consent, physical touch, professional boundaries, training, and accountability.

Consent to take a psychedelic is not a blank check, as far as consent is concerned.

Physical touch is ethically fraught in conventional psychotherapy. Add psychedelic intoxication, disorientation, heightened suggestibility, and a patient asking to be held—what could possibly go wrong?

Patients need explicit boundaries. They also need the ongoing ability to withdraw consent, and independent channels to report misconduct

The therapist’s good intentions are not a safeguarding protocol.

What Five Decades of Addiction Research Taught Me

When I began studying addiction, it was considered a moral failure.

Changing neurotransmission is relatively easy. Producing sustained recovery is considerably harder.

Neuroplasticity is an opportunity, not a clinical outcome. Addiction itself demonstrates that experience-dependent brain plasticity is not invariably beneficial.

Consequently, so far, claims that one psychedelic session can replace years of psychotherapy exceed available evidence.

Psychedelic Patient Safety First
Source: Mark Gold, MD with permission

Patients First

Six decades ago, Leary popularized psychedelic experiences before demonstrating therapeutic value. Today we know better.

The psychedelic trip ends. The biological and psychological consequences may not. Also, if a subsequent issue arises, who responds? Who provides treatment? Who pays? This seems unclear.

Treatment-resistant depression, trauma, PTSD, GAD, and addiction warrant innovative treatments. In contrast, existential uncertainty isn’t a condition requiring pharmacological intervention.

Turn on the science. Tune out the hype. And don't drop the patient.

item.title: Delusions: A Willful and Dangerous Psychotic Symptom
item.description:
Psychosis

Delusions: A Willful and Dangerous Psychotic Symptom

How do intractable, ferocious delusions become part of personal identity?

Posted November 27, 2026

Key points
  • Delusions can become part of identity, making them difficult to relinquish even as insight improves.
  • Unlike hallucinations, delusions are fixed beliefs rather than sensory experiences.
  • Treatment may soften delusional beliefs without fully eliminating underlying suspicions.

I had interviewed James multiple times over a four-month period, at the request of his attorney. I initially examined him two days after he was arrested for stabbing one of his roommates. After arriving home following an evening of drinking and cavorting together, James inexplicably grabbed a knife from the kitchen and viciously attacked one of his roommates before being subdued. Fortunately, the victim survived.

When interviewed by the police, all of James’ roommates described him as “acting weird” for some time. He made cryptic, hostile comments about how he was being “left out” of their plans, which they all said wasn’t true. Still, they emphasized, he was never violent toward them or anyone else.

They all confirmed that, on the night of the attack, large amounts of alcohol were consumed. A blood test completed on the night of his arrest confirmed that James had also used methamphetamines, which he later admitted to using regularly for months.

During my interviews with James, he revealed how he became increasingly convinced that his roommates were not merely socializing without him but were plotting against him. Over time, his suspicion morphed into a fixed delusion that organized his perceptions and the meanings he attributed to their behavior. If they were all out, he assumed that they planned the activity to avoid having to be with him. When they laughed, he believed they were laughing at him. He wondered if they were “plotting something” against him.

Over time, James’ paranoia became increasingly acute. On the day of the stabbing, he was convinced that the victim-roommate arranged for a helicopter to follow his every movement. “I couldn’t even go out in the fresh air… clear my head… I was being followed…”

James suffers from a drug-induced delusional psychosis. Unlike hallucinations, which are sensory-perceptual experiences (e.g., hearing voices that are not there), delusions are false beliefs that have ossified into convictions that are unsupported by objective reality. Psychotic delusions are self-referential, meaning that the individual is at the center of the psychotic belief. For instance, a character on television is believed to be sending messages to oneself, or, in James’ case, the helicopter was following him. This is different from having beliefs that are accepted by certain cultures or religions that seem strange to outside observers.

After months of treatment with psychotropic medication, James began to express some doubts about his paranoid beliefs regarding his roommates, and his agitation lessened. He admitted that it seemed far-fetched that they would have him followed by a helicopter, but still, he was adamant that “something’s going on” with them, and that they harbored ill intent towards him.

With the passage of time and proper treatment, it is not uncommon for delusional beliefs to soften yet continue to have currency in a mind that had been floridly psychotic. This was certainly the case with James, and was the case with other delusional individuals whom I have examined, including those whose delusional beliefs were the result of chronic drug use. Why is this so?

Individuals with chronic schizophrenia frequently suffer from both delusions and hallucinations. They tend to have recurrent episodes of acute psychosis. Their psychotic symptoms are fierce and disruptive, which prompts immediate and intense therapeutic interventions. Symptoms then lessen, and the patient stabilizes, albeit frequently at a lower level of psychosocial functioning. Some patients with schizophrenia will be capable of insight into their distorted thinking during those periods of psychotic remission.

The clinical presentation of those with delusional disorder is quite different. Hallucinations are not a salient feature of the condition or are not present at all. The delusions fester for long periods, while the patient seemingly functions relatively normally. Frequently, the delusions are not as bizarre as James’ belief that his roommates were having him followed by a helicopter. The delusional content may initially appear quite normal, such as a radical political belief. Internally, though, it is much more extreme and reality-distorting. For instance, one might express the belief that a national politician is corrupt, for which there is convincing evidence. Such a rational thought based on objective evidence then becomes reality-distorting and taken to the extreme, such as a conviction that the politician is hypnotizing constituents with his intense stare during his television interviews.

For a formal diagnosis of delusional disorder, the psychotic belief must be present for at least one month. It’s a condition that is relatively rare; delusions that result from long-term drug use are not so uncommon and can cause a major disruption in one’s life, even after a period of sobriety.

Typically, the delusions become increasingly intractable over time. As its longevity as a belief exists in the patient’s mind, so does its conviction as a reality, and its resistance to logic, persuasion, and psychotropic medications.

Why are delusions so enduring and resistant to change? As belief systems, delusions are not sensory-perceptual experiences like hallucinations, which are distinct from a person’s sense of self. An auditory hallucination is frequently experienced as coming from the outside surroundings, or, if internal, as a foreign voice. An enduring delusion takes on the form of a value or a guiding principle. In other words, delusions become part of one’s identity. As such, it is accepted as important to one’s sense of place in the world, and functions to provide meaning in a confusing and ambiguous world.

As I interviewed James over time, I noticed that his rational thinking and reality testing improved, though he resisted an outright rejection of his psychotic beliefs about his roommates. At one point, I commented to him, “You are not ready to give it up,” referring to his beliefs about his roommates. He quietly responded, “Yeah, yeah…yeah.”

Delusions had become part of James’ identity and a way of understanding his world. As with all dimensions of one’s identity and sense of self, change is gradual and takes time.

item.title: A New Way to Bridge Divides During the Holidays
item.description:
Bias

A New Way to Bridge Divides During the Holidays

Self-disclosure, not self-censorship, may increase respect and reduce animosity.

Posted November 27, 2026

Key points
  • In-groups are less closed-minded than members think, yet fear of ostracism can lead to a lack of curiosity.
  • Self-disclosure may reduce animosity between political opponents.
  • Sharing personal experiences can generate greater respect than facts and evidence.
  • A successful political conversation results in greater understanding, not necessarily agreement.

When political differences emerge at family gatherings, we often judge relatives with opposing opinions as ignorant, stupid, crazy, or malicious. Sometimes, we see caricatures, not individuals with unique life experiences that inform their politics.

The usual advice for keeping the peace during the holidays is simple: Keep politics off the table. After all, nobody is likely to change their mind, so debating is useless—and can be unpleasant.

The assumption is that in the game of politics, you win if you persuade people to change their minds and lose if your opponent does. If you change your own mind, it’s game over.

Every so often, I write another post arguing that rather than trying to convince your relatives to change their minds, listening with genuine curiosity is the answer. Here's an additional key to bridging political divides.

New Research on Respect and Connection

International scholars of partisan polarization collaborated to test whether the perception of self-disclosure increased connection, respect, or willingness to interact with political opponents.

Earlier research found that participants across the political spectrum expected that grounding their arguments in facts would earn them greater respect from political opponents. In reality, however, political opponents had greater respect for those who grounded their positions in personal experiences rather than data. Researchers attributed this effect to personal experiences being less readily doubted than the veracity of facts supplied.

Across six studies, research published in 2025 found that participants reported feeling more connected to political opponents and expressed greater respect for them when those opponents’ statements seemed more self-disclosing. “When people self-disclose while sharing their political views,” the studies found, “it breeds connection and bridges divides—a promising strategy to reduce vitriol in an increasingly divided world.”

Misunderstanding Others

Nicholas Epley, author of Mindwise: Why We Misunderstand What Others Think, Believe, Feel, and Want, argues that “introspection makes us feel like we know what’s going on in our own heads, even when we don’t.” A false sense of certainty means we’re also often wrong about what other people are thinking and why they come to their conclusions—especially when we think their ideas are misguided.

Even if we think our own political decisions are fact-based, what underlies our convictions—and the convictions of those with whom we disagree—may be profound existential priorities and universal human concerns. Existential psychiatrist Irvin Yalom calls these “ultimate concerns” such as death, isolation, freedom, and meaninglessness.

Why We Don’t Listen

In 2025, psychologist Todd Kashdan and his colleagues found that Americans underestimate how open-minded and intellectually humble their political in-group actually is. (Yes, their own group.) Regardless of political party, as politically closed-minded as partisans think the other side is, they also misunderstand their own group as being more narrow-minded than it is.

If we believe our own group only sanctions a narrow set of views, it feels risky to be curious about views outside that range. Belonging is a fundamental human need, and ostracism is a profoundly painful human experience that activates some of the same neural systems implicated in physical pain. When a political party becomes an in-group from which we fear exclusion, self-censorship can become a coping strategy.

But we tend to share at least some values and political concerns with those we disagree with. We often prioritize them differently. For example, as I’ve written before: Someone passionate about gun rights may prioritize concerns about government intrusion into freedom and personal autonomy where the right to hunt or defend oneself is concerned, while someone passionate about gun control might be more focused on concerns about the harms caused by firearms to children, such as in school shootings.

Someone passionate about reproductive rights might prioritize concerns about government intrusion into freedom and bodily autonomy, while someone fervently pro-life might be more focused on concerns about harms caused by abortions to unborn babies.

Changing the Game

Kashdan and his colleagues found that once people believe open-mindedness is acceptable to their in-group, they become more willing to be curious; based on that and self-disclosure research, we have new tools available.

When discussing your opinions, talk about your experiences rather than just data. What in your own life has led you to your conclusions? What experiences of harm—in your own life or in the lives of people you know—have shaped your policy preferences? Do your political preferences help you avoid similar harm?

Instead of debating, make curiosity and genuine listening your goal, even for ideas you find obnoxious. Listen for shared concerns, even if prioritized differently. And listen for what you can learn about how your ideological opponents see things.

Nobody’s mind needs changing—although it might happen. But if you learn something you didn't already know about someone at the holiday table, you’ve won the game.

"Listening is a rare happening among human beings,” theologian William Stringfellow in his 1967 book Count It All Joy. “You cannot listen to the word another is speaking if you are preoccupied with your appearance or impressing the other, or if you are trying to decide what you are going to say when the other stops talking, or if you are debating about whether the word being spoken is true or relevant or agreeable. Such matters may have their place, but only after listening to the word as the word is being uttered. Listening, in other words, is a primitive act of love.”

item.title: Capitalism and the Millennial Midlife Crisis
item.description:
Midlife

Capitalism and the Millennial Midlife Crisis

Our options are somehow expanding and shrinking at once in midlife.

Posted November 27, 2026

Key points
  • Capitalism has shaped the midlife crises since the phenomena was identified.
  • The millennial wealth gap is being widened by the current housing and affordability paradigm.
  • Because of this, the midlife crisis is less uniform and more creative--like a choose-your-own-adventure book.
  • It's important to interrogate what you want and why as you buy your way through midlife.

Many studies have shown that the shape of happiness over time is ironically smile-shaped—gradually decreasing until reaching an all-time low at midlife before rebounding. And like the good little consumers we are, we try to spend our way out of the drop. We try to fill the void with shiny things instead of doing the deep inner work needed for self-actualization,

Big purchases have always been a landmark of the midlife crisis. Luxury cars, vacation properties, and other extravagant, ill-advised symbols of the good life are subconsciously used to soothe midpoint ennui. While millennials aren’t immune to this, our relationship with capitalism is more of a complicated situationship than marital bliss, and that changes things.

Millennials are characterized as the first generation who are worse off than their parents. As usual, this headline isn’t the whole picture. What has changed is the spread of wealth. The wealth gap is vast and increasing. So, while some millennials are off buying the classic toys of the midlife crisis, others are struggling to make ends meet, and there is little in between. For struggling millennials, affordability and housing crises have intersected with midlife. So how are most millennials shopping at life’s midpoint?

  • Debt-maxxing — Going into catastrophic debt to keep up with the mid-life Joneses.
  • Buying their first house — What was once considered a starter home is now the forever home. It’s smaller, it costs more, and that’s not all—it also needs more work!
  • Self-soothing with small indulgences — You might never afford a home, but that matcha latte is within reach! Little treat culture makes the everyday bearable for those trying to get by.
  • Going deep into niche hobbies — Forget motorcycles and luxury cars. How about a new e-bike with air-spring shocks and hydraulic brakes?
  • Collecting experiences — Check out how many countries I scratched off my scratch map of the world. Catch ’em all before they fall victim to global warming!
  • Rebelling by downsizing and simplifying — Deciding that the good ol’ American dream ain’t all it’s cracked up to be and turning to fewer goods and more second-hand.

Even if your needs are met, midlife can sometimes mean wishing for something more, better, or different, and there is nothing wrong with that. In fact, it’s quite normal! So, as you decide the choose your own adventure of the modern midlife crisis, here are some questions you might ask yourself:

  • What does a happy and successful life look like to me? How can I get there?
  • What kind of crisis can I afford?
  • What am I drawn to buy, and what is the underlying need or desire? Do I actually want this, or has societal conditioning convinced me I do? Is there another, more affordable way to address the underlying feeling?

Not all midlife-fueled spending is created equal. Some purchases may feel good in the moment but draw you further from your ideal life. And your ideal life may be very different from your peers’ or your parents’. Comparison is the thief of joy; try to avoid it. And if you can’t, at least compare apples to apples. The home you can afford may look much different than the one you grew up in, but it was harder for you to purchase because of factors outside your control. Contextualize and celebrate your achievements.

My midlife splurge has involved buying a rustic off-grid cabin with my friends. Splitting the modest purchase four ways has made it more affordable and more exciting. It’s an investment in the type of future I want: one that centers tranquility and close relationships. I love these people and being away from the chaos of the modern age. This cabin is a symbol of my commitment to them and the sort of life we want to build together. I won’t be drawn in by the mirage of a generic good life. I will decide what fulfillment means to me. I hope you do too.

item.title: Thanksgiving Isn't Over Yet
item.description:
Gratitude

Thanksgiving Isn't Over Yet

Don't miss your chance to "take in the good."

Posted November 27, 2026

Key points
  • The most important part of an experience—a museum or holiday—may be what happens afterwards.
  • Slowing down to "take in the good" can help us honor what we might otherwise miss.
  • The days after Thanksgiving can be time to appreciate the time together, not just rush onto the next holiday.

There’s a riddle in Alain de Botton and John Armstrong’s book Art as Therapy: What’s the most important part of a museum?

Consider that for a second. Maybe it’s the architecture, the explainers on the wall, or the audio tour that helps you make sense of an abstract creation.

No, they suggest: It’s the gift shop.

This is not about surrendering to late-stage capitalism or Black Friday consumerism: It’s about the importance of slowing down to take in the experience you just had. And following a holiday dedicated to gratitude, that’s why this weekend might be the most important part of Thanksgiving.

Source: Sean Drown / Sometimes You Should Be Late / Used With Permission

It’s not over until it’s over

I love museums. They’re amazing places to take in ideas and beauty with other people. But after a world-expanding hour or two, we step back into traffic and chores and, little by little, the magic dissipates.

Enter the gift shop. It’s a chance to travel back in time, to revisit what you just saw and buy a little trinket to keep that experience with you.

That’s the argument for museum gift shops: you’ve just had a lovely experience, but unless you slow down to make meaning of it and take it with you, you risk missing some of its goodness.

Maybe you’ve noticed that Thanksgiving also goes by fast. After all the logistics, planning, meal prep, traveling, and settling in… blink, it’s over. But it doesn’t have to be over, at least not in our minds.

The day itself

I suspect your Thanksgiving wasn’t perfect, but I imagine it had some lovely moments. Here’s one of mine:

On our way to visit my cousin’s family in rural Maryland, we learned that they’d lost power. When we got there, it was still out. So, looking for a way to finish cooking, my cousin’s two Gen Z kids and I ventured out in the pouring rain and gusty wind to find some propane (because, of course, they were out of that, too).

After two failed attempts (one store was out, and the other wouldn’t sell it to us because their power was also out), we miraculously found some at the dollar store. Somewhere in the middle of this little adventure, I found myself sitting in the backseat, expanding my musical horizons with Slayyyter and having a silly time with my cousin’s kids, who, I might add, were being responsible and safe drivers.

It’s the kind of moment that’s easy to miss: the joy of watching the people you love grow up and appreciating how easily we made the most of a power outage.

Oh, and I forgot to mention the best part. Literally the minute we walked in with a full propane tank, returning heroes that we were, the power came back on.

Endings matter

After writing Sometimes You Should Be Late, I’ve become even more fixated on the question of when experiences truly end.

Does yoga class end the moment 9 a.m. hits and we race out and unlock our phones? Or can we take a few minutes to luxuriate in savasana, bask in the glow of sweat, and appreciate that we took time to slow down?

It’s the same with the rest of our lives: we can slow down to complete an experience, or we can rush past it.

I used to do a lot more things back to back to back, at work, on weekends, and on vacation. Here’s what I noticed: sure, I did a lot of activities, but it was harder to fully appreciate them. As I write in my book: “If our timelines leave no room to appreciate the experience we’re having or the people we’re having it with, why bother?”

Take in the good

Slowing down helps us pay attention. It helps us, as psychologist Rick Hanson says, to “take in the good.” He explains that our brains are often like Teflon for positive experiences but magnets for negative ones. Slowing down with the positive helps us rebalance.

What’s particularly interesting about taking in the good is that we don’t have to do this during experiences; we can do it afterward, too.

Here’s the Turkey Day upshot: Thanksgiving Day is over, but the experience of it isn’t.

So, instead of just moving on to the next holiday plan, here’s my invitation: dedicate a little time this weekend to taking in the good of what just happened, muddling imperfectly and all.

Here are three things you might explore:

  1. Reflect on three moments you enjoyed. Take out a journal or a sheet of paper. No need for the moments to be picture-perfect—tender, silly, or meaningful will do.
  2. Write a handwritten thank-you note. Send it to your host, or, if you were the host, to one of your guests. Mention a particular detail or a way they showed up that you appreciated. Sure, text and email are efficient, but writing it out by hand and finding a stamp forces us to slow down.
  3. Share something you’re grateful for. And be specific. Not just “family” or “friends,” but “the way my family can laugh when things go wrong” or “how my friends are such good listeners.”

A weekend to savor

The movie Ferris Bueller’s Day Off offers this reminder: “Life moves pretty fast. If you don’t stop and look around once in a while, you could miss it.”

And here’s the thing: we do have a choice to slow things down at the end, or even a few days afterward, to bring a little more appreciation to the moments of our lives.

That could be a museum visit, a good book, or a day of gathering together—holiday traffic, TSA ground stops, and power outages be damned.

Perhaps the most important part of Thanksgiving is what we choose to do with the experience once it’s over.

Here’s me slowing down with my Thanksgiving gratitude: thanks to my lovely cousin Ann for hosting, for muddling through a Thanksgiving feast without power and keeping it all together, and for raising two responsible kids… er, adults!
